## Conclusion

<!-- Summary of findings. -->
This report used CNN and SNN models to investigate writer identification and pairwise writer verification, respectively, using handwritten digit images from 20 simulated writers across 5 sessions. The tuned CNN achieved a test accuracy of `r cnn_hpo_pct(cnn_hpo_test_accuracy)` compared with a 5% chance-level baseline, indicating that writer identity may be learnable from handwritten images alone, although generalisation to unseen writers remains untested. Similarly, the tuned SNN achieved a test balanced accuracy of `r round(snn_hpo_test_results*100,1)`% for pairwise verification. Its performance was higher for same-session versus different-session pairs (same-session: `r round(same_session$Balanced_accuracy,1)`%; different-session: `r round(different_session$Balanced_accuracy,1)`%), suggesting that session-related variation can make writer verification more challenging. Differences in per-digit performance between the two models, particularly the opposite pattern for digit *2* (the easiest for the CNN, but the hardest for the SNN), highlight the distinct properties of between-writer discrimination and within-writer consistency. Overall, the models provide complementary approaches to learning writer-related features. These findings are limited by the small number of writers, sessions and digits considered, as well as the use of simulated data rather than real handwritten images. Future work could address these limitations by evaluating CNNs and SNNs on larger datasets of real handwriting encompassing a greater diversity of writers, digits and recording sessions.
